data.title: Loud blast at Riyadh airport as travelers evacuated and airlines cancel flights
data.description:
Several wounded in Riyadh airport attack, operations suspended, Saudi aviation authority says

By Timour Azhari and Enas Alashray
Sat, October 10, 2026 at 5:20 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Timour Azhari and Enas Alashray

RIYADH, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Several people were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday that forced a suspension of operations, the ‌country's civil aviation authority said.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, but it comes amid ‌an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis against Saudi Arabia.

Advertisement

The airport had already been struck in two earlier attacks this week that left four ​people dead and exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom's ability to defend itself as it wages war on the Houthis. Saudi Arabia's early warning system did not issue an alert ahead of Saturday's incident.

The Saudi government's media office did not immediately respond to questions from Reuters.

One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. ‌More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing ⁠towards the facility.

An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

US TO "LOOK AT" JOINING SAUDI FIGHT AGAINST ⁠HOUTHIS: TRUMP

Following the attack, US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether the United States planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, ​so we'll ​make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.

The US embassy ​in Riyadh said it was "aware of attacks" and "strongly ‌recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas."

The UK and Irish embassies in Saudi Arabia said in statements on X that they were also aware of a "serious incident" at the airport. The Canadian embassy said that "ongoing military activity" had impacted operations at the airport.

RIYADH DUE TO HOLD MAJOR SUMMITS

Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.

Kuwait Airways said it had cancelled flights to and ‌from the Saudi capital due to what it described as the ​closure of Riyadh airport because of the "security situation" there.

Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways ​earlier cancelled multiple flights between their respective hubs ​and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday.

Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week ‌had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend ​or cancel services to the ​Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.

Organisers of those conferences said on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, and they sought to reassure attendees of their security.

The Houthis have said ​airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it ‌a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group earlier ​this month.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari in Riyadh; Additional reporting by Steve Holland in Washington DC; Writing by Enas ​Alashray and Maya Gebeily;Editing by Gareth Jones and Joe Bavier)

data.title: Trump takes lawsuit against Hillary Clinton over 2016 election to Supreme Court
data.description:
Trump takes suit against Hillary Clinton over 2016 election to Supreme Court

By Andrew Chung
Fri, October 9, 2026 at 11:40 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Andrew Chung

Oct 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year's election by linking his campaign to ‌Russia.

The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers ‌for bringing a "frivolous" suit. A US appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions.

Advertisement

In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the ​Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida.

Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a "false narrative" that he and his campaign colluded with Russia. The lengthy suit alleged "racketeering" and a "conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood," among other claims.

Trump defeated Clinton in that election, despite losing the national popular vote, and served his first term in office from 2017 to 2021.

US government officials have accused Russia of meddling in the 2016 election, ‌and an investigation led by former FBI chief Robert Mueller ⁠documented extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in his favor. Trump has called the idea of Russian interference a "hoax."

Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that year's ⁠election. Trump regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, and has continued to make those false claims.

'POLITICAL MANIFESTO'

US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump's lawsuit against Clinton, citing numerous inadequacies, including that Trump waited too long to bring some of the claims. The judge likened Trump's lawsuit to a "two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him."

Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and ​his ​lead attorney in the case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees and costs, imposing the ​sanctions for bringing a case that the judge said was intended "to dishonestly ‌advance a political narrative." The judge also faulted Trump and his lawyers for a "continuing pattern of misuse of the courts."

Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit used abusive litigation tactics, contained "knowingly false" factual allegations and asserted "frivolous" legal theories.

The Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge's rulings in 2025, including the sanctions.

"Many of Trump's and Habba's legal arguments were indeed frivolous," the 11th Circuit stated.

In court papers, lawyers for Trump and Habba have said that the decisions by the lower courts are having a "profound impact on the presidency, and the nation as a whole."

Mueller, serving as a special counsel appointed by the Justice Department, issued a 2019 report on his investigation. The report stated that Russia "interfered in the 2016 presidential election in ‌sweeping and systematic fashion," but stated that "the investigation did not establish that members of the Trump campaign ​conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities."

Mueller said in his report that he ​found "numerous links" and that the Trump campaign "expected it would benefit" from Russia's effort ​to tilt the ballot in Trump's favor.

Trump's then-Attorney General William Barr appointed a different special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to look into potential ‌missteps by the FBI.

In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the ​FBI lacked "actual evidence" to investigate Trump's 2016 presidential ​campaign and relied too heavily on tips provided by Trump's political opponents to fuel the probe.

Trump's Justice Department last year indicted Comey, one of several adversaries of the president hit with criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after he was accused of lying about authorizing leaks to the news media. ​A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor ‌who Trump handpicked to prosecute Comey had been unlawfully appointed.

Steele, working for an opposition research firm that was hired by a law firm on behalf of ​the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier that alleged ties between Trump's campaign and Russia as well as other salacious accusations, ​all of which Trump denied.

(Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; Editing by Will Dunham)

data.title: Army officials caught off guard by Hegseth's plan to livestream execution
data.description:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth looks on as President Donald Trump speaks to the news media, on the South Lawn of the White House on October 6.
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the execution of the convicted Fort Hood mass shooter would be shown in public caught people across the Pentagon and the Army off guard, three sources familiar with the matter told CNN.

Hegseth made the announcement in an interview with far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday, which he’d visited to give a speech to the crew welcoming them home from their deployment to the Middle East.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said during the interview.

That comment was the first time many in the Army and Pentagon heard about the idea of a firing squad’s execution of Nidal Hasan in Texas being made public, and there were immediately questions about what “public” would mean. There are Army regulations about who can watch a military execution, including family of the prisoner and of the victims, media representatives and a chaplain.

But it was decided by Hegseth, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, and Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell and his staff that “public” would mean it would be livestreamed, one source familiar said. The Pentagon then confirmed as much to the media, saying in a statement, “The Secretary is correct. It will be livestreamed. Details will follow.”

Related article
Nidal Hasan.

Hegseth wants America to watch a firing squad execution. It’s drawing backlash

6 min read

The Army referred questions to the Pentagon, and a Pentagon spokesperson said they had nothing to add beyond Thursday’s confirmation that it would be live-streamed.

The idea has shocked many service members and veterans and provoked a bipartisan backlash. Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday that the livestream could ultimately go forward, saying he didn’t know “if that’s actually going to happen,” but said if it was, “I’m not going to be watching it.”

“It takes away everything America stands for when we do public executions,” one Army officer with multiple deployments to the Middle East told CNN. “The generational harm caused by allowing troops in uniform to stand in front of a man in a wheelchair and watch him get shot to death is irreparable.”

President Donald Trump welcomed the idea of a firing squad execution on Friday.

“We’re giving a man the death penalty who killed 14 soldiers a couple of years ago. Death penalty through firing squad — and he deserves it,” the president said to applause during a White House event honoring Christopher Columbus.

Trump told CNN-affiliate WSTM on Friday he was not involved in the decision to livestream the execution, adding, “but I understand the decision.”

Asked about the livestream by reporters at the White House earlier Friday, the president said his administration would make a determination about it, while reiterating that Hasan will be killed and “through firing squad.” He didn’t answer when a reporter asked if he’d watch the livestream.

FCC chair Brendan Carr told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” it was his understanding that the execution would not be shown on broadcast TV – but that he would defer to Hegseth and “his decisions on how to move forward.”

Many of the details around the livestream have yet to be finalized, and multiple sources told CNN that officials have been working to find answers since it was announced. A second source familiar told CNN that great care is being taken to determine which soldiers would fire on Hasan, taking into consideration the potential psychological impacts of doing so. A specific unit has been selected to carry out the execution, the source said.

Showing the execution on a livestream presents more challenges, the source said, including any effort to obscure from the public the identities of the soldiers involved. It’s also unclear where and if the execution will be streamed beyond the Pentagon’s own website. Broadcasters and social media platforms have strict restrictions on violent and disturbing content.

The first source familiar said there are still questions about whether soldiers can decline to participate, given that the military is moving forward with this as a legal order.

The second source familiar echoed the same, saying while many soldiers may have “taken a life in combat,” this is a very different situation.

“This is a situation where the guy has done a very bad thing and hurt a lot of people, years removed,” the second source said. “He’s going to be immobile and put up like a target.”

data.title: Russian strikes kill 8 in Ukraine a day after Trump's diesel deal with Putin
data.description:
Russian attacks kill 8 in Ukraine after Trump strikes diesel deal with Putin

SUSIE BLANN
Updated Sat, October 10, 2026 at 7:17 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Russia Ukraine War

1 of 6
Rescue workers carry a body after pulling from the rubble of a residential building destroyed by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Kateryna Klochko) (AP Photo/Kateryna Klochko)

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian strikes killed at least eight people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, officials said Saturday, a day after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel that Kyiv warned would help bankroll Moscow's war in Ukraine.

Three children were among the eight people killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the region's defense council, said Saturday. At least 16 people were wounded in the attack.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 55 people over the past four days.

Advertisement

The latest attacks came a day after Trump said he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.

Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Trump's shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.

In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.

"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

According to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Zelenskyy called it "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners."

Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war.

"I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.

data.title: Isaias loses strength, but more than 700,000 are without power in Florida and Alabama
data.description:
Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after Florida landfall, NHC says

By Rhea Rose Abraham and Rajveer Pardesi
Sat, October 10, 2026 at 7:14 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Hurricane Isaias expected to make landfall on US gulf coast

1 of 7
A couple have beers in a hotel lobby during a power outage ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Isaias, in Pensacola, Florida, US, October 9, 2026. REUTERS/Marco Bello

By Rhea Rose Abraham and Rajveer Pardesi

Oct 10 (Reuters) - Isaias weakened to a post-tropical cyclone on Saturday, having rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the ‌Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic ‌season, the US National Hurricane Center said in its latest advisory.

The post-tropical cyclone, crossing over southern Alabama ​after making landfall earlier near Destin, Florida is about 55 miles (89 km) south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kmh), the agency added.

Advertisement

Isaias is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC ‌said.

The center warned of possible ⁠storm surges, urban and river flooding and flash floods across the region, with considerable impacts likely across much of southern Alabama and ⁠the Florida Panhandle into southwest Georgia.

A risk for tornadoes will also persist overnight across the Florida Panhandle and north Florida into southern Georgia, while the tornado threat will continue on Saturday ​across ​parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia, and the Carolinas, ​the agency said.

Alabama's emergency management agency ‌said the hurricane has downed trees and power lines, making travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning.

"Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. "These road closures will remain in effect until conditions are deemed safe for travel."

President Donald Trump, asked ‌about hurricane preparations, told reporters outside the White ​House, "We're watching it very closely, the hurricane," adding ​that it was "under control."

More than 430,000 ​people in Florida and nearly 297,000 in Alabama lost power as ‌the storm hit shore, according to power ​outage tracking firm PowerOutage.us.

"Emergency ​declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X.

Florida's ​emergency services urged residents ‌to shelter in place and watch for hurricane conditions across the north of ​the state.

(Reporting by Rhea Rose Abraham and Rajveer Singh Pardesi in Bengaluru; ​Editing by William Mallard and Ros Russell)

data.title: Boosting U.S. oil supplies with Russian diesel unlikely to have impact on prices, experts say
data.description:
Boosting US oil supplies with Russian diesel unlikely to have much impact on prices, experts say

ALEX VEIGA
Updated Sat, October 10, 2026 at 12:15 AM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Gasoline Prices Colorado

1 of 2
A motorist drives past a sign posting the per-gallon prices for regular unleaded and diesel fuel at a Shell gasoline station Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, in Evergreen, Colo. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski) (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)

A new pact that calls for Russia to boost the U.S. supply of diesel over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.

President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to immediately supply the U.S. more than 300,000 tons of diesel. That would be followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November, then 4 million more tons at some point after that.

The deal marks a stark reversal of policy by the U.S., which from the start of Russia's war with Ukraine had banned imports of Russian oil, and comes at a time when the U.S. economy and consumers are being squeezed by a global rise in oil prices due to the eight-month-long U.S. war with Iran.

Advertisement

The price of diesel has shattered records in recent weeks, ratcheting up inflation for a broad swath of consumer goods.

The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22, according to motor club AAA. It averaged nearly $6.28 a gallon on Friday, up from almost $3.68 this time last year. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too.

Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation for a long list of everyday goods. That's because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks. And some businesses have already passed along steeper costs to consumers in the form of added fees on online orders and packages in the mail.

Shoppers may feel more and more sticker shock, particularly in the grocery aisle. Perishable foods, like meat and produce, face one of the most immediate strains of expensive diesel because they need to be hauled in and restocked frequently — or may be harvested using farm equipment powered by the fuel.

That's turned up the heat on Trump and the Republican Party to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The president's approval ratings on the economy have hit a new low, according to an AP-NORC poll released last week, as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.

A limited impact, at best

Energy policy experts on Friday expressed doubts that a boost in diesel supply from Russia will have a significant impact on oil prices, whether in the U.S. or globally.

"It's kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic," said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics.

"If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they'll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now," Lynch said.

And while the White House may be counting on this move to give some relief at the pump for U.S. truckers, ranchers and farmers who have been hit hard by rising diesel prices, that's not a given.

"The best you could hope for is a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area, Philadelphia maybe," Lynch said. "It just means that the oil is just going to be shuffled around and it's not really going to change the price globally or across the U.S."

If Russia, which in July moved to ban diesel exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries, now believes it is able to resume exports of diesel, then that will help stabilize global diesel prices, said Daniel Sternoff, senior fellow at the Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy.

However, prices are likely to remain elevated overall because a lot of refining capacity in the Middle East isn't available to the world market due to the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz from the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.

"Refined products like diesel are still barely half of prewar levels," Sternoff said. "So, even if there were to be some follow-through from the Russians to put a little extra diesel into the world markets, it might take the edge off of prices, but it will not substantially lower them."

While the deal between Trump and Putin probably won't have much of an impact on prices for diesel consumers in the U.S., it will benefit Russia, said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

That's because Russia is trying to offload its summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and arctic grades that they will need in the coming months, Seigle noted.

"I don't think it'll be enough to materially lower prices in the United States or Europe, but it does certainly let Moscow off the hook in terms of revenue squeeze," he said.

data.title: Trump's new press secretary is a familiar face on Fox News with deep MAGA ties
data.description:
Who is Katie Zacharia, Trump's new White House press secretary?

The president described her as “a devoted fan and member of MAGA.”

Andrew Romano
Fri, October 9, 2026 at 9:20 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Trump announced on Friday that he has chosen Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator, lawyer and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, as his new press secretary. Zacharia replaces Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August.

Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," the president wrote on social media. "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!"

Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on social media. 

To join the White House, Zacharia, 42, will exit her current role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn. Zacharia has also worked with Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State. 

Advertisement

Zacharia is best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol."

In his announcement, Trump said that Zacharia was "involved in my Campaigns, assisting in key Swing States." She wrote in a February New York Post column that she did "hard work helping flip Michigan red in Dearborn" in 2024. 

Zacharia is a California native and self-described "lifelong conservative" who holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University in Malibu. She first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California. 

Citing a source familiar with internal White House discussions, CNN reported on Friday that "Zacharia's selection came about quickly" and that "she was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position."

In her February New York Post column, Zacharia recounted a clash with liberal patrons of her "local cardio kickboxing gym" that ended with the gym owner asking her not to wear her red "Team Trump 2024" hat to exercise class.

"I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent. My constitutional rights aren't negotiable. Tyranny thrives when good people lack courage."

data.title: Trump announces Russian diesel deal weeks after signing sweeping sanctions law
data.description:
Trump says US to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms

MICHELLE L. PRICE and COLLIN BINKLEY
Updated Fri, October 9, 2026 at 6:57 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Gasoline Prices Colorado

1 of 6
The price of a gallon of diesel fuel is shown electronically on a pump at a QuikTrip station Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Greenwood Village, Colo. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski) (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy economy, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.

Advertisement

His move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.

Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel future prices dipped on the news on Friday, the national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.

A terse statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during his call with his U.S. counterpart, he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."

Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."

The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reacted sharply in a social media post, calling it a gift to Putin and saying that the Russian leader was trying to strike "backroom deals" to buy time in the war.

"It plays into Russia's hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

Zelenskyy added in his post: "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."

Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."

"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."

The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.

It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.

This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war.

The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year.

The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine.
